title: Pre-Revenue Startup SR&ED Claim Guide | Canada FAQ
description: Can a pre-revenue startup file an SR&ED claim in Canada? Read our FAQ to learn how early-stage companies earn refundable R&D tax credits.
summary: A pre-revenue startup in Canada can still claim SR&ED tax incentives. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation earns a 35% enhanced investment tax credit on up to $6 million of qualified current expenditures, fully refundable as cash even with zero taxable income, provided Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 are filed within 18 months of year-end.

body.text: A pre-revenue startup in Canada can still claim SR&ED tax incentives. A qualifying Canadian-controlled private corporation earns a 35% enhanced investment tax credit on up to $6 million of qualified current expenditures, fully refundable as cash even with zero taxable income, provided Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 are filed within 18 months of year-end.
1. Executive Summary and Legislative Architecture

Canada's Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program serves as the cornerstone of the federal innovation ecosystem, providing tax deductions and investment tax credits (ITCs) to more than 24,160 businesses annually. Established in its modern statutory structure in 1985 under the Income Tax Act, R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "Act"), the federal SR&ED regime operates through a dual-incentive mechanism. First, Subsection 37(1) of the Act provides an immediate 100% income deduction for qualifying SR&ED expenditures incurred in the current taxation year, alongside the flexibility to carry unused expenditure pools forward indefinitely to reduce taxable income in future taxation years. Second, Subsections 127(5) and 127(9) together with Section 127.1 of the Act provide an Investment Tax Credit ranging from a basic rate of 15% to an enhanced rate of 35% on qualified expenditures, delivered as a reduction of Part I tax otherwise payable, a direct cash refund, or a combination of both, with unused non-refundable ITCs eligible for a three-year carryback and a 20-year carryforward.

Between late 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian research and development tax landscape underwent its most profound legislative expansion in more than a decade. Following multi-stage policy consultations initiated in Budget 2024—which also launched consultations toward a federal patent box regime designed to encourage intellectual property retention in Canada—and preliminary legislative proposals outlined in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement that committed an estimated $1.9 billion over five years beginning in 2024–2025, the federal government enacted sweeping structural enhancements in Budget 2025 through Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1, S.C. 2026, c. 3), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. These legislative reforms fundamentally recalibrate corporate R&D economics across Canada for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024). Specifically, Bill C-15 doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% refundable ITC from $3 million to $6 million—surpassing the $4.5 million intermediate limit initially proposed in the 2024 Fall Economic Statement—thereby increasing the maximum annual enhanced cash refund from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000. Concurrently, the legislation raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from the $10 million to $50 million corridor to an expanded range of $15 million to $75 million, extended eligibility for the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time in program history, and reinstated full SR&ED income deductibility and ITC eligibility for capital property acquired and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024.

Simultaneously, provincial R&D tax regimes have undergone major structural realignment to reflect evolving capital intensity and commercialization priorities. Most notably, Quebec abolished its legacy suite of wage-based, university, and consortium R&D tax credits (including the long-standing Form RD-1029.7 wage credit) for fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025, replacing them with the unified, harmonized Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC) under sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Quebec). Concurrently, Ontario restored capital expenditure eligibility across its provincial R&D tax credits in the 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement, and British Columbia made its provincial SR&ED tax credit permanent in 2026 while aligning with the federal $6 million limit, public corporation access, and capital expenditure restoration.

body.text: 2. Statutory Definition of SR&ED and Judicial Jurisprudence
2.1 Subsection 248(1) and Statutory Exclusions

The legal threshold for determining whether technical activities qualify for Canadian R&D tax incentives is governed by the definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act, a statutory foundation that remained untouched even as Bill C-15 expanded financial limits and eligible expenditure categories. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED comprises a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. The statutory architecture divides primary qualifying investigations into three core branches: basic research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view; applied research, which encompasses work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view; and experimental development, which encompasses work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Once a foundational project satisfies the criteria of basic research, applied research, or experimental development, supporting activities—strictly confined by statute to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research—also qualify as SR&ED to the extent that the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of the core scientific or technological investigation.

To prevent routine commercial engineering, post-development production, and general business operations from drawing tax subsidies under Section 37 and Section 127, subsection 248(1) explicitly excludes seven enumerated categories of work from constituting SR&ED across paragraphs (e) through (k). Specifically, paragraph (e) excludes market research or sales promotion; paragraph (f) excludes quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; paragraph (g) excludes research in the social sciences or the humanities; paragraph (h) excludes prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; paragraph (i) excludes the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; paragraph (j) excludes style changes; and paragraph (k) excludes routine data collection. Furthermore, administrative policy enforced by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) dictates that the eligibility of any SR&ED project ceases immediately upon the project completion date. The completion date is legally defined as the earliest point at which the claimant achieves the scientific or technological advancement by resolving the associated uncertainties, determines that the scientific or technological uncertainties cannot be resolved, or terminates the project for any commercial or technical reason.
2.2 The Foundational Common Law Test: Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies

While subsection 248(1) establishes the statutory text, Canadian tax jurisprudence has distilled the definition of SR&ED into a binding five-question judicial test. In the landmark Tax Court of Canada decision Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CarswellNat 696, then Judge (later Chief Justice) Bowman articulated the analytical criteria for evaluating whether claimed activities constitute SR&ED and outlined the purposive approach that courts must take to give effect to Parliament's intent in enacting the incentive. This five-question framework was formally adopted as binding appellate precedent by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. The Queen, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740, [2001] F.C.J. No. 1886 (QL) (at paragraph 17), affirming 2000 DTC 2372. The Northwest Hydraulic and C.W. Agencies framework has subsequently been reaffirmed across the entirety of Canadian SR&ED case law, including National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. Canada, R&D Pro-Innovation Inc. v. The Queen (2014-1594(IT)G, 2015), Emotion Picture Studios Inc. v. The Queen, 2015 TCC 323, Flavor Net Inc. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 179, Clevor Technologies Inc. v. Her Majesty the Queen, 2019 TCC 166 (per Justice Russell at paragraph 11), and Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025).

body.text: To discharge the legal burden of proof on a balance of probabilities and demolish the Minister of National Revenue's assumptions, a claimant must satisfy all five criteria concurrently. First, the project must confront a genuine technological risk or uncertainty that cannot be resolved through "routine engineering," which Chief Justice Bowman defined as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field. Second, the claimant must formulate specific hypotheses—defined as ideas consistent with known facts that serve as a starting point for further investigation—expressly aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty. Third, the procedure adopted must accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, encompassing a structured cycle of formulating, testing, and modifying hypotheses through experiment or analysis rather than unguided trial and error. Fourth, the investigation must seek and result in a technological advancement that advances the general understanding of scientific relations or technology or advances the taxpayer's technological knowledge base. Crucially, the jurisprudence establishes that the technological advancement achieved only needs to be slight to qualify as SR&ED, and the definitive falsification of a hypothesis through failed experimentation still generates qualifying technological advancement by establishing why a specific technical approach cannot succeed under defined constraints. Fifth, a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results must be kept as the work progresses, serving as a natural by-product of the scientific method.
2.3 Evidentiary Nuances in Tax Court Litigation

Recent Tax Court of Canada decisions illustrate how rigorously the judiciary enforces the causal nexus between hypothesis formulation, systematic progression, and contemporaneous evidence. In a notable software development appeal (2020 TCC 47), the corporate appellant claimed SR&ED expenditures for its "PTS Project," which sought to develop a web-based, cross-platform, and cross-browser compatible application integrating dynamic pivot tables within a multi-tier architecture (MTA) comprising ADO, Classic ASP, COM+, and SQL Server 2000 rather than SQL Server 2005. The lead developer, Mr. Saini, testified that existing literature on web pivot tables only functioned in static environments and had never been combined with an MTA framework. He explained that the team first attempted to use section variables and cookies to store data and make processing appear instantaneous, and when that failed, attempted a second method of temporarily storing and hiding data at the browser level. In evaluating the claim, the Tax Court found (at paragraph 43) that specific technological uncertainties existed given the architectural constraints. Furthermore, addressing the fifth Northwest Hydraulic criterion (at paragraphs 65–67), the Court explicitly held that maintaining a detailed written record is not an explicit statutory mandate in the Income Tax Act or its Regulations, meaning documentary evidence is not strictly mandatory and oral testimonial evidence is legally admissible, albeit risky. Nevertheless, the Court dismissed the appeal because Mr. Saini's testimony failed to demonstrate a "logical progression between each test and preceding or subsequent tests," resulting in a fatal failure to satisfy the third criterion of a systematic investigation.

A parallel evidentiary standard governs hardware and materials engineering claims, as demonstrated in the Tax Court of Canada decision in Docket 2008-3875(IT)G (decided June 11, 2010) concerning a plastic sheet thermoformer ("Jentel"). The appellant performed custom thermoforming of enclosures, displays, and tote bins using moulds, vacuums, and air pressure, and claimed 2005 SR&ED expenditures for developing a lighter, smaller "Multi-Bin" storage system requiring less manufacturing labour and transport energy. During development, the appellant conducted load testing across various materials (concluding aluminum was best suited), tested three different moulds constructed from different casting materials alongside multiple iterations of groove design in an unsuccessful effort to manufacture a consistent part groove, and applied a heat sink during thermoforming. The Tax Court dismissed the appeal and awarded costs to the Respondent, ruling that evaluating hundreds of plastics, comparing thermoforming flexibility against injection moulding mould costs, iterating groove geometries, and employing a heat sink constituted routine engineering and standard procedures accessible to competent professionals rather than a systematic investigation aimed at technological advancement. Conversely, where a claimant maintains structured experimental records linking specific processing parameters to hypothesis testing—as occurred in Manning Canning Kitchens Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2025), where the Minister had disallowed 2020 taxation year food-processing expenditures under subsection 248(1)—the Tax Court held (at paragraph 31) that the taxpayer successfully discharged its burden on a balance of probabilities across all five Northwest Hydraulic questions and allowed the appeal in full.
2.4 Evolution of CRA Administrative Guidelines: The "Why and How" Framework

For several decades, the CRA administered technical eligibility reviews under Information Circular IC 86-4R3, a publication that Judge Bowman recognized in Northwest Hydraulic as a generally useful administrative authority. During its earlier SR&ED policy clarification initiative, the CRA consolidated IC 86-4R3 into the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy, which explicitly mirrored the five common law questions established in Northwest Hydraulic.

In August 2022, however, the CRA archived the Eligibility of Work Policy and promulgated modernized Guidelines on the Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Tax Incentives. While the CRA and the Federal Court of Appeal have both confirmed that the underlying statutory definition in subsection 248(1) did not change and that Northwest Hydraulic remains the binding legal interpretation of SR&ED, the 2022 administrative guidelines reorganized the CRA's field audit methodology into two streamlined requirements known as the "Why" and the "How". The "Why" requirement evaluates the scientific or technological purpose of the project—specifically, whether the work is conducted in order to advance scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement by overcoming an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty. The "How" requirement evaluates the methodology of the project—specifically, whether the work is conducted by means of a systematic investigation or search carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. Under the CRA's guidelines, satisfying the "How" requirement entails four integrated operational stages: first, the generation of a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving an objective or resolving a problem, expressed as a proposed method, approach, or solution); second, the testing of that idea or hypothesis by means of experiment or analysis, allowing the hypothesis to evolve as testing progresses; third, the development of logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis; and fourth, the keeping of contemporaneous evidence generated as the work progresses.
3. Federal SR&ED Financial Mechanics and the 2025–2026 Reforms
3.1 The 2025–2026 Legislative Overhaul (Bill C-15)

The enactment of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026—implementing the Budget 2025 SR&ED reforms and codified in the CRA's updated SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy (dated October 7, 2026)—introduced five transformative enhancements to the federal program. First, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (on or after December 16, 2024), the maximum annual pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures eligible for the enhanced 35% ITC rate doubled from $3 million to $6 million. This expansion doubles the maximum annual enhanced refundable cash credit from $1,050,000 to $2,100,000 for qualifying corporations and associated corporate groups that share the annual expenditure limit.

Second, Bill C-15 significantly expanded the corporate size phase-out thresholds under subsection 127(10.2). Historically, a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC) saw its enhanced expenditure limit reduced if its prior-year taxable income exceeded $500,000 (phasing out completely at $800,000) or if its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeded $10 million (phasing out completely at $50 million). While Budget 2019 repealed the use of taxable income as a factor in determining a CCPC's expenditure limit for taxation years ending after March 19, 2019, the $10 million to $50 million taxable capital phase-out remained a barrier for mid-sized, capital-intensive enterprises. Following the review of taxable capital thresholds initially announced in Budget 2022 and rescheduled in subsequent fiscal updates, Bill C-15 raised the taxable capital phase-out thresholds for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to $15 million and $75 million of taxable capital employed in Canada across all CCPCs in an associated group in the preceding taxation year (referencing the Part I.3 large corporations tax principles in IT-532 ARCHIVED).

Third, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Parliament extended the enhanced 35% refundable ITC on up to $6 million of qualified expenditures to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs), as well as to "eligible subsidiaries" resident in Canada where not less than 90% of the issued shares of each class of capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more ECPCs. Previously, public corporations were restricted exclusively to the basic 15% non-refundable ITC. For ECPCs, the $6 million expenditure limit is shared among members of a consolidated corporate group that prepare consolidated financial statements (presenting assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows as a single economic entity) and phases out linearly when the corporation's or consolidated group's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years lies between $15 million and $75 million. If an entity joins or leaves a consolidated group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the year in question. Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs may also formally elect to calculate their expenditure limit phase-out using this three-year average annual gross revenue method (aggregating the financial statement revenue of all associated group members over the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether the corporations were associated throughout that entire period) instead of the taxable capital method.

Fourth, reversing the 2014 legislative repeal of capital claims, Bill C-15 reinstated full SR&ED eligibility for capital expenditures on property acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as lease and rental costs incurred after that date. Qualifying capital property—including specialized research tools, laboratory apparatus, testing and prototyping equipment, manufacturing machinery, and IT/GPU compute infrastructure for artificial intelligence and machine learning—now qualifies both for immediate 100% deduction within the Section 37 expenditure pool and for ITC generation under Section 127. To qualify, the capital property must be new to the claimant's business, used in Canada, and intended to be used all or substantially all of its operating time over its expected useful life for SR&ED. While current expenditures within the $6 million limit earn a 100% refundable 35% ITC for qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs, ITCs earned on eligible capital expenditures are 40% refundable (with the remaining 60% credited as non-refundable ITCs).

Fifth, Budget 2025 and Bill C-15 mandated administrative modernization at the CRA, including the integration of artificial intelligence into internal claim routing and the launch, effective April 1, 2026, of a voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process designed to confirm project technical eligibility before expenditures are incurred and reduce processing times for approved claims from an average of 180 days down to 90 days.
3.2 Expenditure Limit Phase-Out Formulas and Corporate Control Traps

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a qualifying CCPC (or associated group of CCPCs) that uses the default taxable capital method calculates its annual SR&ED expenditure limit based on its prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada according to the following linear reduction formula (prorated for short taxation years):

Expenditure limit = $6,000,000 × ($75,000,000 − A) ÷ $60,000,000, where A is the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada (if A is $15,000,000 or less, the limit is $6,000,000; if A is $75,000,000 or more, the limit is nil)

Under this formula, the full $6,000,000 expenditure limit remains intact until prior-year taxable capital reaches $15,000,000, after which every $10 of additional taxable capital reduces the expenditure limit by $1 until the limit reaches nil at $75,000,000. Where an ECPC computes its limit—or where a CCPC elects the gross revenue test—the variable A in the equation above is replaced by R, representing the average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years.

From a corporate governance and M&A perspective, maintaining CCPC status remains a paramount compliance priority for private companies that are not listed on a designated Canadian stock exchange as an ECPC. Under the Income Tax Act, CCPC status depends not merely on current voting share ownership, but on de jure and statutory deemed control rules. If a private Canadian technology or life sciences company enters into a shareholders' agreement, convertible note, or option arrangement that grants non-resident investors or a foreign parent corporation a contingent right to acquire control of the company, the corporation can lose its CCPC status immediately upon signing—even if non-residents hold less than 50% of the issued shares—instantly collapsing its federal SR&ED entitlement from a 35% refundable cash credit to a 15% non-refundable tax credit.

body.text: To illustrate the quantitative impact of the Bill C-15 framework, a qualifying CCPC incurring $6,000,000 in qualified current SR&ED expenditures in a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 earns $2,100,000 in total ITCs ($6,000,000 at 35%), all $2,100,000 of which is paid as a 100% refundable cash credit—representing an $870,000 (+70.7%) increase in cash refundability (from $1,230,000, being $1,050,000 on the first $3,000,000 plus 40% of the $450,000 basic credit on the remaining $3,000,000) and a $270,000 (-100%) reduction in non-refundable credits compared to the pre-December 16, 2024 rules. Where that same qualifying CCPC scales its qualified current SR&ED expenditures to $8,000,000 in the taxation year, the first $6,000,000 earns the 35% enhanced rate for $2,100,000 in 100% refundable credits, while the remaining $2,000,000 earns the 15% basic rate for $300,000 in ITCs, of which 40% ($120,000) is refundable in cash and 60% ($180,000) is non-refundable, yielding $2,220,000 in total immediate cash refunds alongside $180,000 in carryforward tax credits. Note also that under section 127, no amount may be included in a claimant's ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax (referencing paragraph 149(1)(j) for non-profit R&D corporations).
4. Qualifying Expenditures (QREs), Overhead Methods, and Pool Reductions
4.1 Categories of Eligible SR&ED Expenditures

Under subsection 37(1) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, only specific statutory categories of expenditures incurred in Canada directly in respect of SR&ED may enter the federal deduction and ITC pools. The primary expenditure category consists of salaries and wages under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i), which captures 100% of the remuneration paid to employees directly engaged in performing or directly supporting SR&ED in Canada. Claimants must maintain contemporaneous time sheets, project allocation matrices, and payroll records to substantiate the precise proportion of each employee's working hours dedicated to eligible SR&ED activities. The second core category comprises materials consumed or transformed, which captures 100% of the cost of raw materials, chemical reagents, electronic components, or supplies that are either completely consumed or physically transformed into a non-commercial state during experimental testing or prototype fabrication.

The third category governs arm's-length Canadian subcontractors under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii) and paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9). Where a taxpayer pays an arm's-length contractor to perform SR&ED in Canada on the taxpayer's behalf, 100% of the eligible contract expenditure is deductible in computing income under subsection 37(1), but only 80% of the eligible contract payment is included in the "qualified expenditure" pool under subsection 127(9) to earn the 35% or 15% federal ITC. When claiming contractor expenditures, the claimant must explicitly describe the contractor's work in the technical project narrative on Form T661, confirm that the work was performed on its behalf in Canada, and retain the executed contract and statement of work for CRA inspection. Conversely, if the claimant itself performed SR&ED on behalf of another business on a contract basis (excluding joint or collaborative research where each party bears its own costs), the claimant must report that fact on Form T661 and reduce its qualified expenditures by the contract payments received or receivable so that two taxpayers do not claim SR&ED ITCs on the same underlying work.

The fourth category encompasses capital expenditures and lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024 under Bill C-15 (replacing the historical pre-2014 regime that had included first-term and second-term shared-use equipment under subsection 127(9)). To claim capital property—such as specialized research tools, testing apparatus, manufacturing prototypes, or GPU and compute servers used in machine learning—the property must be newly acquired after December 15, 2024, used in Canada, and intended to be used all or substantially all for SR&ED. However, tax practitioners and auditors must carefully navigate a statutory timing nuance highlighted in Bill C-15's amendments to subsection 127(11.2) of the Act. While immediate expense deductibility under Section 37 applies on its face to capital expenditures made after December 15, 2024, subsection 127(11.2) governs when property is deemed to have been acquired for the purpose of computing SR&ED ITCs, requiring strict verification of acquisition and available-for-use dates, purchase orders explicitly marked "for R&D purposes," dedicated general ledger cost centres, and contemporaneous equipment usage logs. Additionally, subsection 127(8) through 127(8.2) governs the allocation of SR&ED qualified expenditure pools and ITCs for partnerships, restricting a limited partner's ITC allocation to the partner's at-risk amount at the end of the partnership's fiscal period (reduced by any clean economy tax credit allocations under subsection 127.47(1)).
4.2 Overhead Election: Proxy Method vs. Traditional Method

Taxpayers must elect annually on Form T661 between two mutually exclusive statutory methods for capturing SR&ED overhead expenditures—the Proxy Method (Prescribed Proxy Amount, or PPA) and the Traditional Method. Once filed with the CRA for a given taxation year, the chosen method is irrevocable for that year.

body.text: 4.3 Government Assistance, Non-Government Assistance, and Pool Grinding

Under subsection 37(1) and the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, a claimant's deductible SR&ED expenditure pool and qualified SR&ED expenditure pool must be reduced by the amount of any government assistance or non-government assistance that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive in respect of the SR&ED expenditures at the time of filing. Subsection 127(9) defines government assistance broadly to capture any monetary contribution or financial benefit of any kind (other than a prescribed financial benefit or an ordinary tax deduction) from a government, municipality, or other public authority, whether delivered as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax, or investment allowance.

Consequently, direct federal and provincial innovation grants (such as NRC IRAP contributions or Alberta Innovates grants) as well as provincial R&D tax credits (such as the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit, the Quebec CRIC, the Manitoba R&D tax credit, or the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant) constitute government assistance that reduces ("grinds") the federal Section 37 deductible pool and the federal Section 127 qualified expenditure pool before the 35% or 15% federal ITC is computed. Furthermore, any federal SR&ED ITC claimed to reduce Part I tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduces the Section 37 deductible SR&ED expenditure pool in the subsequent taxation year, and subsection 127.1(3) deems any refunded SR&ED ITC to have been deducted under subsection 127(5), thereby reducing the balance of ITCs available for carryback or carryforward. Conversely, where a corporation subsequently repays government assistance or contract payments that previously reduced its allowable SR&ED expenditure pool, the repayment qualifies as an eligible SR&ED expenditure in the taxation year in which the repayment is made.
5. Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes
5.1 Comprehensive Provincial and Territorial Comparison

Beyond the federal SR&ED program, nine Canadian provinces and one territory provide complementary R&D tax credits. With the exception of Quebec (which is administered separately by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (which is administered separately by Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered centrally by the Canada Revenue Agency through provincial schedules filed alongside the federal T2 Corporation Income Tax Return. Prince Edward Island, the Northwest Territories, and Nunavut do not offer separate territorial or provincial R&D tax credits. Additionally, in provinces such as Saskatchewan, registered agricultural producers contributing check-off levies to commodity organizations (such as the Saskatchewan Barley Development Commission, SaskCanola, Saskatchewan Pulse Growers, Sask Wheat, and the Prairie Oat Growers Association) can claim a designated percentage of their non-refunded levy (for example, 53.5% federally and 29% provincially in historical SaskBarley allocations) as pooled SR&ED tax credits.

body.text: 5.2 Deep-Dive Jurisdiction Analysis
5.2.1 Quebec: Abolition of Legacy Credits and Launch of the CRIC (2025–2026)

For fiscal periods and taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, the Government of Quebec enacted a landmark structural overhaul of its provincial R&D tax incentive system under the Taxation Act (Quebec). Specifically, Quebec abolished five legacy R&D tax credits (as well as industrial design tax credits): the tax credit for R&D salaries and wages (historically claimed on Form RD-1029.7), the tax credit for university research or research carried out by a public research centre or a research consortium, the tax credit for private partnership pre-competitive research, the tax credit for fees and dues paid to a research consortium, and the tax credit for technological adaptation services. None of these five legacy credits may be claimed for a taxation year or partnership fiscal period beginning after March 25, 2025.

In their place, Quebec introduced the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), codified at sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act (Quebec). Whereas the legacy RD-1029.7 regime was restricted primarily to R&D wages (offering up to 30% on $3 million of wages for SMEs) and imposed an intricate, asset-based per-employee exclusion threshold (formerly up to $83,333 per employee), the new CRIC establishes a single, fully refundable tax credit open to all corporations and qualified partnerships that carry on business in Quebec and maintain an establishment in Quebec. Crucially, the CRIC expands the scope of qualifying activities beyond traditional SR&ED to include pre-commercialization activities carried out in Quebec, and broadens the eligible expenditure base to encompass salaries and wages, consideration paid to subcontractors, payments to eligible research organizations, and capital expenditures for the acquisition of property. After deducting a unified CRIC exclusion threshold, the CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit of 30% on the first $1,000,000 of eligible expenditures and 20% on all eligible expenditures exceeding that $1,000,000 threshold, irrespective of whether the corporation is a CCPC, public company, or foreign-controlled subsidiary.
5.2.2 Alberta: The Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Introduced effective January 1, 2021 to replace the former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit, the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is governed by sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act and administrative guidance in Information Circular IEG-1R4 (revised April 2025). Despite being styled a "grant," the IEG is a refundable corporate income tax credit administered through the Alberta corporate tax system without a separate grant application. Qualified corporations claim the IEG by filing AT1 Schedule 29 (and AT1 Schedule 29 Listing) with the Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return (AT1) within 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (that is, 21 months after the end of the taxation year). Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) processes IEG disbursements only after the underlying expenditures—which must have been incurred in Alberta after December 31, 2020 and match federal SR&ED eligibility rules, including the Alberta proxy amount and repayments of prior government assistance—have been verified by the CRA and confirmed by TRA to have been carried out in Alberta. Partnerships, trusts, and individuals are statutorily excluded from claiming the IEG.

The IEG utilizes a two-tier incremental calculation on up to $4,000,000 in annual eligible Alberta R&D spending (allocated among associated corporations and prorated by the ratio of days in the taxation year to 365, or 366 if the year includes February 29). Under paragraph (a) of the statutory formula, the corporation earns a base payment of 8% on the lesser of its eligible Alberta expenditures for the taxation year and its maximum expenditure limit. Under paragraph (b), the corporation earns an additional 12% (bringing the total enhanced rate to 20%) on the amount by which the lesser of its eligible Alberta expenditures and its maximum expenditure limit exceeds its base level of spending. The base level of spending is defined as the corporation's (or associated group's) average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the preceding two taxation years, expressed as (E1 + E2) ÷ 2, where E1 and E2 are the eligible Alberta expenditures of the first and second preceding taxation years. For example, if an unassociated corporation claiming the IEG had eligible Alberta expenditures of $8,000 and $12,000 in its two preceding taxation years, its base level of spending is $10,000 (($8,000 + $12,000) ÷ 2), meaning it earns 8% on the first $10,000 and 20% on all spending above $10,000 up to $4,000,000 (yielding a maximum annual cash grant of $800,000 where the two-year base is zero).

Significantly, IEG rates and 100% cash refundability apply equally to CCPCs and foreign-controlled corporations (non-CCPCs), provided the corporation maintains a permanent establishment in Alberta and has prior-year taxable capital below $50,000,000. When the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation (or associated group for its last taxation year ending in the preceding calendar year) lies between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out linearly under Information Circular IEG-1R4 as follows:

where A is the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada; if A is less than $10,000,000, A is $10,000,000, and if A exceeds $50,000,000, A is $50,000,000, reducing the expenditure limit to nil at $50,000,000 of taxable capital. Additionally, if property included in an IEG claim is subsequently disposed of or converted to commercial use (either directly by the claimant under Situation 1 or by a transferee in a non-arm's-length transfer under Situation 2), sections 26.95–26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act trigger a recapture addition to Alberta tax otherwise payable. As illustrated in Information Circular IEG-1R4, if a corporation had $5,000,000 of eligible expenditures in 2021 (capped at the $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit), earned $340,000 in IEG (an 8.5% effective rate on the $4,000,000 limit), included $100,000 of acquired property in that pool, and sold the property in 2022 for $20,000, the 2022 recapture added to Alberta tax payable is the lesser of $1,360 ($20,000 × 8.5% × $4,000,000 ÷ $5,000,000) and $6,800 ($100,000 × 8.5% × $4,000,000 ÷ $5,000,000), resulting in a $1,360 tax addition.
5.2.3 Ontario, Manitoba, British Columbia, and Saskatchewan Nuances

Ontario administers three distinct corporate R&D tax credits through the CRA (for taxation years after December 31, 2008) for corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario. First, the Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) provides an 8% fully refundable tax credit (reduced from 10% for taxation years starting after May 31, 2016) on up to $3,000,000 of qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (a maximum annual cash refund of $240,000). The $3,000,000 OITC expenditure limit phases out when the corporation's (or associated group's) prior-year taxable income is between $500,000 and $800,000 or when its prior-year taxable capital is between $25,000,000 and $50,000,000. Second, the Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC) provides a 3.5% non-refundable credit (reduced from 4.5% after May 31, 2016) on eligible Ontario expenditures after deducting any OITC or OBRITC, with no expenditure cap. Third, the Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC) provides a 20% fully refundable credit on qualified contract payments to eligible Ontario research institutes, capped at $20,000,000 of expenditures per associated group. Crucially, the 2026 Ontario Fall Economic Statement (ON FES 2026) restored eligibility for capital expenditures under both the OITC and the ORDTC to mirror federal Bill C-15. Because the OITC and ORDTC do not reduce one another's statutory base except as prescribed, but do reduce the federal SR&ED qualified expenditure pool, Ontario corporations may file a written waiver of the OITC or ORDTC within six months of their taxation year-end (or on an amended return).

In Manitoba, section 7.3 of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba) provides a 15% R&D tax credit (reduced from 20% after April 11, 2017) claimed on Schedule T2SCH380 within one year after the corporation's T2 filing due date (18 months after year-end). For in-house SR&ED carried out in Manitoba, exactly half of the credit (7.5%) is refundable in cash and the remaining 7.5% is non-refundable (subject to a 3-year carryback and 20-year carryforward against Manitoba income tax payable), whereas R&D performed under contract with qualifying research institutes is 100% refundable. Notably, while a corporation can renounce its Manitoba credit provincially up to one year after its filing due date, for federal SR&ED pool purposes the Manitoba credit must be formally renounced on or before six months after the corporation's taxation year-end. In British Columbia, the 10% BC SR&ED tax credit was made permanent in 2026 and harmonized with Bill C-15, offering 100% refundability on up to $6,000,000 of expenditures (including reinstated capital expenditures) for both CCPCs and ECPCs. In Saskatchewan, sections 63 to 63.4 of The Income Tax Act, 2000 (Saskatchewan) provide a 10% credit claimed on Schedule T2SCH403, which is 100% refundable for CCPCs on the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures (up to $200,000 cash) and non-refundable thereafter, subject to an overall annual cap of $1,000,000 in total credits per year.
5.3 Combined Federal-Provincial Stacking and Pool-Grinding Mechanics

Because provincial R&D tax credits constitute government assistance under subsection 127(9) of the Income Tax Act, applying provincial and federal tax credit rates to the same gross expenditure pool overstates the combined credit. Instead, the provincial credit reduces the federal qualified expenditure pool prior to computing the 35% or 15% federal ITC. Denoting gross qualified expenditures by E, the provincial rate by p, and the federal rate by f, the net combined effective credit rate is expressed as:
Combined credit rate = p + f × (1 − p), so that total combined credits = E × [p + f × (1 − p)]

Notice also the stark cash-flow divergence for pre-revenue foreign-controlled subsidiaries: because their 15% federal ITC is non-refundable, the $150,000 provincial refund in Atlantic Canada (or up to $800,000 under the Alberta IEG, or 20%–30% under the Quebec CRIC) represents the only cash arriving in the first year.
5.4 Non-Dilutive Grant Stacking (NRC IRAP, Alberta Innovates, ERA, and Mitacs)

Canadian corporations routinely layer direct non-dilutive innovation grants onto their federal and provincial SR&ED tax credit stacks. Whereas SR&ED tax credits retrospectively reimburse completed research after the taxation year-end, direct grants provide prospective funding for upcoming project milestones. Although any grant funding received or entitled to be received for SR&ED-eligible tasks must be deducted as government assistance from the Section 37 and Section 127 pools, the 55% federal Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) is computed on gross eligible SR&ED salaries prior to deducting salary grants, enabling stacked claims to recover 55% to 75%+ of total R&D expenditure.

At the federal level, the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP) serves as the flagship direct R&D salary subsidy for SMEs, providing contributions of up to $500,000+ per project (with empirical program data showing 2,025 agreements in Alberta alone, a median firm award of $75,000, and a middle-half award range of $50,000 to $194,900), alongside its IP Assist sub-stream (median award $15,800, middle-half range $10,000 to $22,730). Complementary federal programs include CanExport Innovation (median award $11,777, middle-half range $6,090 to $19,838), CanExport SMEs (up to $50,000, median award $25,000), the Regional Artificial Intelligence Initiative (RAII) administered by regional development agencies such as PrairiesCan, Investments in Forest Industry Transformation (IFIT) (up to $10,000,000), Mitacs AI Advantage (ADOPT and AI+X streams providing $10,000 to $25,000 awards per research intern), and the Canada Small Business Financing Program (CSBFP) (providing up to $1.15 million in term financing). At the provincial level in Alberta, Alberta Innovates (operating on a $256 million annual budget across a tech ecosystem of 167,000+ small businesses and 108,000 tech workers in Calgary and Edmonton) offers the Venture Development Grant ($10,000 to $150,000 covering up to 75% of project costs) and the Agriculture & Food Innovation Grant (up to $750,000), while Emissions Reduction Alberta (ERA) (which has invested over $965 million since inception) funds heavy industrial decarbonization through its Industrial Transformation stream ($500,000 to $10,000,000 per project), complemented by workforce upskilling under the Canada-Alberta Productivity Grant (renamed from the Canada-Alberta Job Grant in 2025, covering up to $5,000 per trainee and $100,000 per employer per fiscal year when applied for at least 30 days prior to training).
6. Governing Authorities, Filing Compliance, Audit Workflow, and Dispute Resolution
6.1 Statutory Filing Deadlines and Prescribed Forms

The federal SR&ED program is administered by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), while legislative tax policy is developed by the Department of Finance Canada. To access both the Section 37 income deduction and the Section 127 ITC, a claimant must file prescribed forms containing all prescribed information with the Minister of National Revenue (via mandatory Corporation Internet Filing for applicable corporations). Corporate claimants must submit Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim)—using the updated version of Form T661 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024—together with Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) alongside their T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (while partnerships file Form T5013 and Quebec Form TP-600-V).

Under subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the Income Tax Act and the CRA's SR&ED Filing Requirements Policy, the absolute statutory reporting deadline for filing Form T661 and Schedule T2SCH31 is 18 months from the end of the taxation year in which the SR&ED expenditures were incurred (equivalent to 12 months after the 6-month corporate T2 filing due date). For instance, for a corporate taxation year ending December 31, 2024, the absolute statutory deadline is June 30, 2026. As confirmed in Tax Court jurisprudence (including Docket 2015-3982(IT)G, decided January 24, 2017), subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) operate as a strict statutory bar: the CRA possesses no administrative discretion to grant extensions, and failure to file the prescribed forms with all prescribed project and financial fields by the 18-month deadline permanently extinguishes the taxpayer's entitlement to the deduction and ITC for that year. Consequently, best audit practice dictates filing the SR&ED claim at the 6-month T2 due date or well in advance of the 18-month deadline to leave a protective window for responding to CRA completeness queries.

body.text: 6.3 CRA Technical and Financial Audit Workflow and Escalation Hierarchy

Upon filing, every SR&ED claim is initially assessed at the CRA Tax Centre. While low-risk claims may be accepted as filed, claims flagged by the CRA's risk-assessment system (which integrates AI-supported administration following Budget 2025) are routed to a Coordinating Tax Services Office, where the Control Centre determines whether the claim requires a desk review or a comprehensive field audit by a Research and Technology Advisor (RTA), a Financial Reviewer (FR), or both. Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA also implemented internal workflow reforms to remove redundant review steps, curb excessive documentation requests, and accelerate determinations on claim adjustments.

When a claim is selected for detailed review, the claimant should designate both a knowledgeable technical contact who personally participated in the SR&ED work and a financial contact who understands the underlying cost accounting. The RTA reviews current and prior claim submissions, requests clarifying technical evidence, and, where a site visit is warranted, transmits an advance list of projects and documents to be examined at the claimant's premises. At the conclusion of the site visit, the RTA is required by CRA procedure to provide the claimant with a preliminary verbal indication of eligibility determinations and any outstanding technical concerns so the claimant can submit supplemental representations before the RTA issues the written SR&ED Review Report. Concurrently, the FR conducts a financial audit in accordance with the SR&ED Program Financial Claim Review Manual (verifying T4 payroll registers, contractor agreements, capital usage logs, and government assistance, as well as ensuring payroll compliance where TEI/CRA audit protocols apply) and collaborates with the RTA to issue a formal CRA Proposal Letter.
Where a claimant disagrees with the findings of an RTA or FR, the CRA and the Income Tax Act establish a strict five-tier escalation hierarchy:

items: Tier 1 (Reviewer Rebuttal): The claimant first engages directly with the assigned RTA or FR to clarify technical facts, provide additional contemporaneous records, and resolve misunderstandings prior to finalization of the Proposal Letter.

Tier 2 (Managerial Escalation): If discussions with the reviewer reach an impasse, the claimant escalates the dispute to the Research and Technology Manager (RTM) or the Financial Review Manager (FRM) overseeing the audit team.

Tier 3 (Administrative Second Review): If managerial intervention does not resolve the concern, the claimant may request an Administrative Second Review conducted by the Assistant Director, SR&ED at the Tax Services Office to evaluate whether the audit adhered to CRA policy and procedural fairness.

Tier 4 (CRA Appeals Branch — Notice of Objection): Once the CRA issues a formal Notice of Assessment or Reassessment, the claimant's right to informal SR&ED branch review ends, and the claimant must initiate the formal statutory dispute process by filing a Notice of Objection with the CRA Appeals Branch within 90 days of the assessment date.

Tier 5 (Tax Court of Canada and Federal Court of Appeal): If the CRA Appeals Branch confirms the reassessment or fails to vacate it, the taxpayer may appeal to the Tax Court of Canada (TCC)—where the taxpayer bears the burden of demolishing the Minister's assumptions on a balance of probabilities under the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—with further appellate recourse to the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA).

body.text: 7. Strategic Synthesis and Actionable Audit Recommendations

The enactment of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside Quebec's transition to the CRIC and the restoration of capital expenditure eligibility in Ontario and British Columbia, fundamentally reshapes corporate R&D tax strategy across Canada. To capture the full financial benefit of these reforms while fortifying claims against CRA and Revenu Québec audit challenges, corporate tax directors, CFOs, and engineering leaders should immediately implement four integrated compliance protocols.

First, mid-market CCPCs and newly eligible Canadian public corporations (ECPCs) must re-model their associated and consolidated group structures under the expanded $6 million expenditure limit and the $15 million to $75 million phase-out corridor. Specifically, asset-intensive CCPCs in manufacturing, biotech, medical devices, and clean technology whose balance-sheet taxable capital exceeds $15 million—or previously exceeded the former $50 million cutoff—should evaluate electing the newly enacted three-year average gross revenue calculation method for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024. Where a CCPC has substantial invested capital from equity financings or equipment on its balance sheet but modest trailing three-year revenue, electing the gross revenue test can preserve 100% of its $6 million expenditure limit and unlock up to $2.1 million per year in refundable federal cash credits. At the same time, private corporations raising cross-border venture capital must conduct a rigorous legal review of all shareholders' agreements and convertible instruments prior to closing to ensure non-resident investors are not granted contingent options or rights that could inadvertently strip the corporation of CCPC status.

Second, finance and engineering teams must overhaul capital procurement and fixed-asset accounting to capitalize on the post-December 15, 2024 restoration of capital expenditures and lease costs. Because qualifying machinery, laboratory apparatus, prototyping equipment, and AI/ML GPU compute clusters must satisfy the strict statutory requirement that the property be new and intended to be used all or substantially all for SR&ED in Canada (and must satisfy the timing rules of subsection 127(11.2)), organizations cannot commingle commercial production hardware with R&D hardware. Claimants should update internal chart-of-accounts cost centres, explicitly annotate purchase orders and lease agreements with "Acquired for SR&ED Purposes," document exact acquisition and available-for-use dates, and maintain automated machine-utilization logs demonstrating experimental usage.

Third, multi-provincial enterprises must realign their provincial tax filings to capture newly expanded provincial bases while avoiding statutory recapture and pool-grinding traps. In Quebec, corporations and partnerships with fiscal periods beginning after March 25, 2025 must retire legacy Form RD-1029.7 wage-only tracking and implement project cost accounting for the new CRIC (sections 1029.8.21.16.1 to 1029.8.21.16.31 of the Taxation Act), capturing not only R&D wages and subcontractors but also capital property acquisitions and pre-commercialization activities to maximize the 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million above the exclusion threshold (and 20% on excess spending). In Alberta, corporations claiming the 8% to 20% Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) on AT1 Schedule 29 must track two-year rolling expenditure averages to optimize incremental spending timing and monitor subsequent asset dispositions carefully to prevent unexpected recapture additions under Information Circular IEG-1R4. In Ontario and British Columbia, claimants should incorporate post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures into their OITC, ORDTC, and BC SR&ED schedules following the 2026 provincial harmonization updates.

Finally, R&D teams must embed contemporaneous scientific documentation directly into their daily engineering workflows and leverage the CRA's April 2026 Voluntary Pre-Claim Approval Process. As confirmed by the Tax Court of Canada in 2020 TCC 47 and 2008-3875(IT)G, oral testimony or retrospective summaries that fail to prove a systematic, logical progression from technological uncertainty and hypothesis formulation through iterative testing to analytical conclusions will result in total claim disallowance. By configuring version-control repositories, ticket-tracking systems, and laboratory notebooks to record hypotheses and experimental test results in real time—and by submitting major or emerging-technology R&D plans to the CRA's Pre-Claim Approval Process prior to project commencement—Canadian innovators can secure upfront technical eligibility certainty and accelerate cash refund disbursement to a 90-day cycle.
